country.name: Oregon
country.summary: Oregon is the cool, rain fed counterweight to California on the American West Coast: a state whose reputation rests on Pinot Noir from the Willamette Valley, with Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and a growing band of sparkling wines beside it. Its growers planted the modern vineyards from the mid 1960s, looked to Burgundy rather than Napa for their model, and wrote labelling rules stricter than the federal ones. The exam asks for the Willamette Valley and its nested AVAs, the shape of the state's southern valleys, the shared AVAs along the Columbia and the Snake, and the percentages on an Oregon label. Hold the valley first, then the rest of the state as context.
country.overview:
Oregon's wine country divides into three. The Willamette Valley, south of Portland between the Coast Range and the Cascades, is the cool western heart and the home of Pinot Noir. The southern valleys, the Umpqua and the Rogue with the Applegate inside the Rogue, are warmer and drier, and grow Tempranillo, Syrah and the Bordeaux varieties as well as Pinot Noir in their cooler corners. The Columbia corridor in the north and east is shared with Washington: the Columbia Gorge, the Columbia Valley and the Walla Walla Valley all cross the state line, and the Snake River Valley in the far east is shared with Idaho.

The modern story begins in the mid 1960s, when a handful of growers trained in California came north to find a climate cool enough for Pinot Noir and planted the Dundee Hills and the valley's other slopes. A Burgundy house followed in 1987 with an estate of its own, and the valley's reputation was made by small family estates working together rather than by a few large houses. That cooperative habit shows in the state's rules, written by the growers themselves.

The law is the federal AVA system with a stricter Oregon layer on top. Where a federal label needs 75 percent of the named variety, an Oregon label needs 90 percent for most varieties, with a list of mostly Bordeaux and Rhône grapes allowed at 75 percent. An AVA named on an Oregon label calls for 95 percent of its grapes from that AVA, and the word Oregon alone calls for all of them. A vintage calls for 95 percent of the year named.

For the exam, the Willamette Valley carries the weight: the AVA itself, the nested AVAs on its hillsides, the three soil families and the Pinot Noir style. The southern valleys and the shared AVAs are asked as geography, and the labelling percentages are asked as numbers, so learn them as a short list and say them aloud.
ladder: A federal appellation of origin defined by geography, carrying no quality rank and no rule on grapes or yields.
A smaller AVA inside a larger one, such as the Dundee Hills inside the Willamette Valley; a wine may use either name if it meets the percentage.
Oregon as the place of origin: every grape from the state under the Oregon rule, against 75 percent federally.
labels: All of the grapes from Oregon.
At least 95 percent of the grapes from the AVA named.
At least 90 percent of the variety named, the Oregon rule for most grapes.
Grown, made and bottled by the producer on land it controls, in one AVA.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The state's signature, grown mainly in the Willamette Valley in a red fruited, savoury and medium bodied style.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.styles: The leading white by volume, made dry and fuller than Italian Pinot Grigio, with pear and a soft texture.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown in the Willamette Valley from Burgundian clones, lean and mineral with restrained oak.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small planting in the cooler sites, made dry to off dry with sharp acidity.

exam: Name the three parts of the state: the Willamette Valley, the southern valleys and the Columbia corridor.
Know which AVAs cross a state line and with which neighbour.
Give the Oregon labelling percentages for variety, AVA, state and vintage.
Place Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay as the state's leading grapes.
traps: The Oregon variety rule is 90 percent, not the federal 75, and the exam asks the stricter number.
Walla Walla Valley is mostly in Washington, but its AVA crosses into Oregon.
Pinot Gris here is a dry, fuller white, not a thin Pinot Grigio style.
The Snake River Valley is shared with Idaho, not with Washington.

questions.q: Which grape is Oregon's signature variety?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir made the state's reputation in the cool Willamette Valley; the three distractors are warm climate grapes that mark California more than Oregon.

questions.q: Under the Oregon rule, what is the minimum share of the named variety for most grapes?
questions.exp: Oregon asks 90 percent of the variety named for most grapes, stricter than the federal 75; the 85 and 95 figures belong to the AVA rules.

questions.q: Which AVA does Oregon share with Idaho?
questions.exp: The Snake River Valley crosses from eastern Oregon into Idaho; the other three are the AVAs shared with Washington along the Columbia.

questions.q: Which two valleys make up Southern Oregon?
questions.exp: The Southern Oregon AVA takes in the Umpqua Valley and the Rogue Valley, warmer and drier than the Willamette, with the Applegate Valley nested inside the Rogue.

questions.q: What share of grapes must come from a named AVA on an Oregon label?
questions.exp: Oregon asks 95 percent from the AVA named, ten points above the federal 85, the same stricter habit as its variety rule.

questions.q: Which mountain range shelters the Willamette Valley from the Pacific?
questions.exp: The Coast Range stands between the valley and the ocean and takes the worst of the weather; the Cascades close the valley on its eastern side.

questions.q: In which decade were the first modern Pinot Noir vineyards planted in the Willamette Valley?
questions.exp: The first modern plantings went into the Dundee Hills in the mid 1960s by growers who had trained in California and wanted a cooler home for Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Willamette Valley (OR)
regions.summary: The Willamette Valley is Oregon's heartland for Pinot Noir, a long cool valley running south from Portland between the Coast Range and the Cascades. Its wines are built on marine air, volcanic and sedimentary hillsides and a harvest that often finishes under autumn rain. Pinot Noir leads, with Pinot Gris and Chardonnay beside it, in a style lighter and more savoury than most of California. A server should hold the nested AVAs, the strict Oregon labelling rules and the Burgundian roots of its growers, who planted the first modern vines in the Dundee Hills in the mid 1960s and have kept a cooperative, small estate culture since.

terroir.climate: Cool and maritime. The Coast Range takes the worst of the Pacific weather, the Van Duzer Corridor lets cool evening air through to the Eola-Amity Hills, and long mild summers ripen Pinot Noir slowly. Winters are wet, summers are dry, and rain at harvest is the perennial hazard that makes vintages vary.
terroir.soils: Three soil families matter. Red volcanic Jory lies on the Dundee Hills, marine sedimentary Willakenzie on the Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge slopes, and windblown Laurelwood loess over basalt on the Chehalem Mountains. The valley floor carries deep silts left by the Missoula floods and is largely avoided for fine wine.
terroir.topography: A broad valley some 150 miles long, with vines on the hillsides between roughly 200 and 1,000 feet, mostly on south and east facing slopes above the fog of the floor.
terroir.water: The Willamette River runs north through the valley to the Columbia. Its tributaries carve the hill ranges, and the Pacific, forty miles west, shapes the climate more than any river does.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Red cherry, cranberry and forest floor, medium bodied with bright acidity and fine tannin, from the Dundee Hills' plush fruit to the firmer wines of the Eola-Amity Hills.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.styles: The leading white, made dry, with pear, apple and a rounder texture than Italian Pinot Grigio.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Dijon clones on cool sites give a lean, citrus and mineral wine with careful oak, the valley's second serious wine.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small planting on the cooler slopes, dry to off dry, with sharp acid and lime.

wines.note: Red cherry and cranberry with a savoury, earthy edge, light tannin and fresh acidity. Serve lightly cool, around 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, with salmon, duck or mushroom dishes.
Dry, with pear and a soft, slightly oily texture. Serve well chilled with shellfish, light fish courses and salads.
Lean and citrus led, with a mineral finish and quiet oak. Serve cool, not cold, with roast chicken, cream sauces and firm white fish.
Traditional method from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, crisp and bready. Serve cold as an aperitif or with fried and salty courses.

made.viticulture: The valley's growers plant on the hillsides, not the floor, because the slopes drain and sit above the morning fog. Pinot Noir is trained on vertical trellises at moderate density, with Dijon clones alongside the older Pommard and Wädenswil selections that the first growers brought in. The hazards are rain at flowering and at harvest, a cool year that leaves fruit short of ripeness, and the birds that strip early ripening sites. Growers pick by taste as much as by sugar, usually in late September and October, and many farm organically or biodynamically on small holdings. Site matters: the choice of soil family, slope and height above the floor marks the wine as clearly as the clone, and the nested AVAs were drawn to say so. Dry farming is common on the deeper soils, while the shallow volcanic sites may irrigate young vines only.
made.winemaking: Pinot Noir is made in the Burgundian manner: destemmed or part whole cluster, a cool soak, gentle punch downs, and ageing in French oak with a modest share of new barrels so the fruit stays in front. Chardonnay is pressed whole, fermented in barrel, and left on its lees with little or no new oak, in a leaner style than the valley made in its early years. Pinot Gris is made cold in stainless steel to keep its pear fruit, usually dry. Sparkling wines use the traditional method from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with time on the lees before disgorgement. The valley's houses are small, so single vineyard and single AVA bottlings are common, and blending across the valley is the choice of the larger estates rather than the rule.

law.classification: The Willamette Valley is a federal AVA, a boundary drawn on geography with no quality ranking. Inside it sit nested AVAs on the hill ranges, each a smaller boundary a wine may use when it meets the percentage. Oregon adds its own stricter layer to federal labelling: 90 percent of the named variety for most grapes, 95 percent from a named AVA, every grape from Oregon when the state alone is named, and 95 percent of a named vintage. There is no cru system; the hierarchy a server speaks of is the hierarchy of names on the label, from Oregon to Willamette Valley to a nested AVA to a single vineyard.
tiers: The whole valley, established in the 1980s; 95 percent of the grapes from inside it when named.
A hill range inside the valley, such as the Dundee Hills or Ribbon Ridge; the same 95 percent rule applies to the smaller name.
A named site within a nested AVA, no legal tier but the top of the valley's own ladder of names.
labels: At least 95 percent of the grapes from the AVA.
At least 90 percent of the variety under the Oregon rule.
No legal meaning in Oregon; a house's own word for its chosen barrels.

places.name: Dundee Hills
places.note: The valley's founding hills, on red volcanic Jory soil, where the first modern Pinot Noir was planted in the mid 1960s. The wines are plush, red fruited and the valley's most recognised.

places.name: Yamhill-Carlton
places.note: A horseshoe of marine sedimentary Willakenzie slopes west of Dundee, warmer and drier, giving darker fruit and fuller Pinot Noir.

places.name: Ribbon Ridge
places.note: A small ridge of marine sediment sitting inside the Chehalem Mountains, with fine grained, aromatic Pinot Noir from its uniform soils.

places.name: Chehalem Mountains
places.note: The highest ground in the valley, carrying all three soil families, so its wines vary from site to site more than any other nested AVA.

places.name: Laurelwood District
places.note: The loess over basalt slopes on the north side of the Chehalem Mountains, drawn as a nested AVA in 2020.

places.name: Eola-Amity Hills
places.note: Hills in the path of the Van Duzer Corridor, where afternoon Pacific wind thickens skins and gives firm, structured Pinot Noir with bright acidity.

places.name: McMinnville
places.note: The foothills of the Coast Range south west of the town, on shallow marine soils, giving dark fruited and savoury wines.

places.name: Van Duzer Corridor
places.note: The gap in the Coast Range that funnels ocean air into the valley, recognised as a nested AVA in 2019 for its windy, cool sites.

producers.name: The Eyrie Vineyards
producers.why: The founding estate of modern Oregon Pinot Noir, planted in the Dundee Hills in the mid 1960s.

producers.name: Domaine Drouhin Oregon
producers.why: A Burgundy house's Dundee Hills estate, founded in 1987, the clearest sign that Burgundy took the valley seriously.

producers.name: Bergström Wines
producers.why: A family estate in the Chehalem Mountains known for single vineyard Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

exam: Place the valley between the Coast Range and the Cascades, south of Portland.

traps: The valley floor is not where the fine wine grows; the hillsides are.
Jory is volcanic, Willakenzie is marine sediment; the exam swaps them.
Oregon Pinot Gris is dry and fuller, not a thin Pinot Grigio.
The Oregon rule is 90 percent of the variety, not the federal 75.

questions.q: Which soil is the red volcanic soil of the Dundee Hills?
questions.exp: Jory is the weathered basalt of the Dundee Hills; Willakenzie is marine sediment, Laurelwood is loess over basalt, and the Missoula silts lie on the valley floor.

questions.q: Which nested AVA lies in the path of the Van Duzer Corridor?
questions.exp: The Eola-Amity Hills take the afternoon wind that comes through the Van Duzer gap in the Coast Range, which thickens skins and firms the tannin.

questions.q: Which grape leads the Willamette Valley?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir is the valley's signature; Syrah and Tempranillo belong to the warmer southern valleys and Merlot to the Columbia corridor.

questions.q: Which mountain range closes the valley on its eastern side?
questions.exp: The Cascades stand to the east and the Coast Range to the west; the Siskiyous and the Blue Mountains lie in the south and the north east of the state.

questions.q: What is the marine sedimentary soil of Yamhill-Carlton called?
questions.exp: Willakenzie is the marine sandstone and siltstone of the Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge slopes, against the volcanic Jory of the Dundee Hills.

questions.q: In which nested AVA were the valley's first modern Pinot Noir vines planted?
questions.exp: The founding plantings of the mid 1960s went into the Dundee Hills, which remain the valley's most recognised nested AVA.

questions.q: Which white grape is the Willamette Valley's leading white variety?
questions.exp: Pinot Gris is the valley's leading white by volume, made dry and fuller than Italian Pinot Grigio, with Chardonnay rising behind it.
